docs.title: Image Views
docs.text: A Vulkan image view describes how the image data should be accessed and used by the graphics pipeline and shaders. This includes images such as in the swap chain, textures, or framebuffers. On average, a graphics card can support up to 16 image views.

docs.title: References
docs.text: https://docs.vulkan.org/tutorial/latest/03_Drawing_a_triangle/01_Presentation/02_Image_views.html

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Vulkan is an API developed by the Khronos Group that includes cross-platform support and is heavily optimized for performance.

Boilerplate behind Vulkan is extremely verbose, requiring managing every detail related to memory, setup, hardware, and even explicitly controlling communication between the Vulkan API and the OS window library to draw things on screen.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
To include Vulkan C++ headers and its RAII bindings, we use the following code.

#if defined(__INTELLISENSE__) || !defined(USE_CPP20_MODULES)
#include <vulkan/vulkan_raii.hpp>
#else
import vulkan_hpp;
#endif

VS Code’s IntelliSense engine flags import vulkan_hpp as an error so we default to using #include <vulkan/vulkan_raii.hpp>. When CMake USE_CPP20_MODULES is defined, we used import vulkan_hpp for a compiling speed up. Otherwise, we default to #include <vulkan/vulkan_raii.hpp> once again.

docs.title: References
docs.text: https://docs.vulkan.org/tutorial/latest/00_Introduction.html https://docs.vulkan.org/tutorial/latest/03_Drawing_a_triangle/00_Setup/00_Base_code.html

docs.title: Pipelines
docs.text: A Vulkan pipeline (VkPipeline) is an immutable object that describes the entire process of how a GPU should convert data to final pixels.

docs.title: The Graphics Pipeline
docs.text:
A standard graphics pipeline is outlined as follows:

Input Assembler

Collects raw vertex data and assembles them into geometric primitives like points, lines, or triangles.

↓ Vertex Shader

Runs code on each vertex to perform transformations on them.

↓ Tessellation (Optional)

Allows subdivision of geometry.

↓ Rasterization

Converts geometric primitives to fragments (pixel candidates) overlapping the screen.

↓ Fragment Shader

Runs code on each fragment to calculate the final color, lighting, and textures.

↓ Color Blending

Mixes the final pixel values with the existing data inside the framebuffer (and handling transparency).

docs.title: References
docs.text: https://docs.vulkan.org/tutorial/latest/03_Drawing_a_triangle/02_Graphics_pipeline_basics/00_Introduction.html

docs.title: Queues
docs.text: In Vulkan, command buffers are sent asynchronously through Vulkan queues.

docs.title: Queue Families
docs.text: A queue family represents a set of queues that support a specific set of operations. The support for these queue families can also be validated when selecting a physical device.

docs.title: References
docs.text: https://docs.vulkan.org/tutorial/latest/01_Overview.html https://docs.vulkan.org/tutorial/latest/03_Drawing_a_triangle/00_Setup/04_Logical_device_and_queues.html

docs.title: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization
docs.text:
Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII), is a programming concept where a resource's lifecycle is tied to a local variable's lifetime. The constructor first acquires the resource, then after it is automatically destroyed and the resources are cleaned up.

In Vulkan, RAII is used very commonly used throughout an application to solve the challenge of manual resource management in such a verbose API in C++. Therefore, we use Vulkan's official RAII bindings.

Vulkan RAII objects can be retrieved with the vk::raii namespace containing RAII wrapper classes.

docs.title: The Vertex Shader
docs.text: The vertex shader inputs raw vertex data including its position, color, and texture coordinates and transforms each vertex. The output is the final clip position and any needed per-vertex data. The final positions, after the clip positions undergo perspective division and the viewport transform, are then sent to the rasterizer to convert the primitives the vertices form into pixel fragments.

docs.title: Clip Position
docs.text: The clip position, or clip coordinate is the final 4D transformed vertex position calculated in the vertex shader. These clip positions are found after the GPU clips all vertices that sit outside the camera's view.

docs.title: Perspective Division
docs.text: Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) are 3D coordinates found through the perspective division step, where clip positions are divided by its 4th dimension (divided by $w$, where the vector is defined as $(x, y, z, w)$). In turn, the framebuffer is mapped to $[-1, -1]$ by $[1, 1]$.

docs.title: The Viewport Transform
docs.text: In the viewport transform, NDC coordinates are converted to screen coordinates that exactly match the framebuffer resolution. The final 2D screen coordinates are then returned along with the corresponding per-vertex depth data to be sent to the rasterizer.

docs.title: The Fragment Shader
docs.text: The fragment shader runs on every fragment returned by the rasterizer. It computes the final color and visual properties of an individual pixel before displaying on screen.

docs.title: Shader Compiling
docs.text: Vulkan expects all shaders to be in SPIR-V bytecode. SPIR-V is a binary intermediate representation (a universal, pre-compiled bytecode format) that provides universal optimization and cross-platform compatability, especially with extensions. Because SPIR-V is a pre-compiled format, it can be compiled from high-level shader languages such as GLSl or HLSL.

docs.text: https://docs.vulkan.org/tutorial/latest/03_Drawing_a_triangle/02_Graphics_pipeline_basics/01_Shader_modules.html https://docs.vulkan.org/guide/latest/what_is_spirv.html https://learnopengl.com/Getting-started/Coordinate-Systems

docs.title: The Logical Device
docs.text: The Vulkan logical device is a handle for the physical device that abstracts all communication between the GPU and the Vulkan API.

docs.title: References
docs.text: https://docs.vulkan.org/tutorial/latest/01_Overview.html https://docs.vulkan.org/tutorial/latest/03_Drawing_a_triangle/00_Setup/04_Logical_device_and_queues.html

docs.title: The Physical Device
docs.text:
The Vulkan physical device bridges the gap between the Vulkan API and physical hardware, or GPUs.

To select a physical device, we test if it is compatible with the Vulkan API, any extensions, queue families, and any other required features or properties. We can also rank GPUs by "score" depending if it is most suitable and most performant for our needs.

docs.title: References
docs.text: https://docs.vulkan.org/tutorial/latest/03_Drawing_a_triangle/00_Setup/03_Physical_devices_and_queue_families.html

docs.title: The Swap Chain
docs.text: Because Vulkan provides no default framebuffer that automatically refreshes, we must explicitly manage, clear, and synchronize our own framebuffer to present something on screen. As such, the Vulkan swap chain is used. The Vulkan swap chain is an explicit queue of renderable framebuffers that will be presented to screen while synchronized to the refresh rate of the screen. In other words, it swaps rendered images in its queue to the window surface.

docs.title: Presentation Modes
docs.text: The presentation mode a surface uses describes how images should be swapped to the presentable screen.

docs.title: vk::PresentModeKHR::eImmediate
docs.text: In this mode, swap chain images are displayed immediately the moment when the GPU finishes a new frame. Because the GPU doesn't necessarily wait for a frame to completely finish, it may result in screen tearing. This mode results in the lowest latency out of all presentation modes.

docs.title: vk::PresentModeKHR::eFifo
docs.text: In this mode (where FIFO means First In, First Out), the swap chain is a queue of images where the screen displays images refreshed from the FIFO queue. When the queue is full, it blocks the application. This mode is also known as vertical sync, or V-Sync, where waiting for the frame to completely finish eliminates screen tearing. This mode results in low latency, although slightly more than vk::PresentModeKHR::eImmediate due to the GPU blocking when the queue is full.

docs.title: vk::PresentModeKHR::eFifoRelaxed
docs.text: Similarly to vk::PresentModeKHR::eFifo, the swap chain in vk::PresentModeKHR::eFifoRelaxed is a queue of images where image refreshes are blocked until processes are finished. However, if the GPU is late to a frame, that frame is swapped to the window surface immediately. Because it doesn't wait for any screen processes to finish, it may cause visible screen tearing. This mode results in lower latency than vk::PresentModeKHR::eFifo in situations when the GPU lags behind the monitor.

docs.title: vk::PresentModeKHR::eMailbox
docs.text: This mode is another variation of the vk::PresentModeKHR::eFifo except when the queue is full, images already in the queue are replaced with newer frames. Commonly known as triple buffering, this mode usually uses more energy while avoiding screen tearing. It result in lower latency than vk::PresentModeKHR::eFifo because the GPU is never blocked.

docs.title: The Swap Extent
docs.text:
The swap extent, or the resolution of the swap chain images has the exact same dimensions as the resolution of the window surface. Because Vulkan uses pixels by convention, the swap chain image resolutions must also be in pixels.

For GLFW, we must use glfwGetFramebufferSize to get the exact window resolution in pixels, or otherwise screen coordinates used by GLFW by default will result in a resolution mismatch (in high DPI displays).

docs.title: Surface Formatting
docs.text: The format of a surface defines the displayed color space and its color precision (color depth) or color formatting.

docs.title: Color Spaces
docs.text:
Common color spaces used for surface formatting include VK_COLOR_SPACE_SRGB_NONLINEAR_KHR or sRGB formats such as VK_FORMAT_B8G8R8A8_SRGB or VK_FORMAT_R8G8B8A8_SRGB with automatic gamma correction.

Note: In sRGB formats, it is important to note that the final image before displaying must contain linear sRGB values!

(More on color spaces can be found in the official documentation.)

docs.title: References
docs.text: https://docs.vulkan.org/tutorial/latest/03_Drawing_a_triangle/01_Presentation/01_Swap_chain.html

docs.title: The Vulkan Instance
docs.text: The Vulkan instance connects the application to the Vulkan API. Specifically, it bridges this gap through initializing any Vulkan drivers, API extensions, application specifications, debug (i.e. validation layers) and retrieving data about the physical device.

docs.title: References
docs.text: https://docs.vulkan.org/tutorial/latest/01_Overview.html https://docs.vulkan.org/tutorial/latest/03_Drawing_a_triangle/00_Setup/01_Instance.html

docs.title: Validation Layers
docs.text:
Because Vulkan is designed to be as memory efficient and performant as possible, the one thing on defafult the API critically lacks are error checks and validations. Thus, bugs in the code will often cause silent errors or unexpected crashes. Therefore, Vulkan added its own system called validation layers.

Validation layers can be enabled with Vulkan's SDK VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation. To access its debug messenger callback features that actually print out the details we use the object vk::raii::DebugUtilsMessengerEXT.

docs.title: References
docs.text: https://docs.vulkan.org/tutorial/latest/03_Drawing_a_triangle/00_Setup/02_Validation_layers.html

docs.title: Window Surface
docs.text:
Vulkan is platform agnostic, meaning it was designed as an open, industry-wide standard without it being tied to any specific operating system or company. Therefore, to connect the Vulkan API to an operating system's window, we will use Window System Integration (WSI) extensions.

To include GLFW, we can use the GLFW's Vulkan compatibility extensions with the macro GLFW_INCLUDE_MACRO along with glfwCreateWindowSurface to actually create the Vulkan surface.

#define GLFW_INCLUDE_VULKAN
#include <GLFW/glfw3.h>

docs.title: References
docs.text: https://docs.vulkan.org/tutorial/latest/03_Drawing_a_triangle/01_Presentation/00_Window_surface.html
